speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: MR. McGRATH-CONSTRUCTION OF OIL REFINERY AT COME-BY-CHANCE-MANNER OF RELEASE OF STOP-ORDER STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, notice of which has been given to Your Honour in accordance with the Standing Order. My question of privilege, in my view, affects the rights of all hon. members of the House.
Yesterday the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries released a statement to the Press Gallery in which the minister announced that a "stop-order" had been issued on the construction of the new oil refinery at Come-by-Chance, Newfoundland, in accordance with the provisions of sections 33(1) and 33(2) of the Fisheries Act. This is a very important statement and one that should have been made in the House in accordance with well-established practice. The minister does have the right to make a statement outside the House. My question of privilege, however, is based on the fact that the minister did not release copies of the statement to members of the House until this morning, thereby denying us the right to question the minister in the House yesterday. There is provision in the rules under Standing Order 41(2) to table statements in the House. The minister, in failing to do so and in failing to provide members of the House with copies of his statement at the time of its release to the press, in my opinion, is guilty of flagrantly violating the rules and practices of the House. If Your Honour rules that I have a prima facie question of privilege, I would move that the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. McGRATH-CONSTRUCTION OF OIL REFINERY AT COME-BY-CHANCE-MANNER OF RELEASE OF STOP-ORDER STATEMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John's East has given the Chair notice of his intention to raise this matter by way of an alleged or suggested breach of the privileges of the House. With respect, I must advise the hon. member and the House that, after having given the matter due consideration, because the hon. member had given the Chair notice of his intention to raise this matter, I find it difficult to agree with the contention of the hon. member that this matter should be considered by a committee of the House.
The hon. member claims that copies of the minister's statement should have been distributed to hon. members so that they could have been given an opportunity to ask questions in the House. It seems to me, without trying to pass judgment on whether or not the statement should have been made in the House, that the questions that could have been asked yesterday can be asked today. There will be a question period in a short while, and I
would think that the hon. member will have the same rights today as he had yesterday.
I recognize, as does the hon. member, that under the provisions of Standing Order 41(2) a minister of the Crown is entitled to table certain documents. However, the Standing Order does not provide that the minister is obligated to table a statement and there is no provision in the Standing Orders to the effect that a statement should be made in the House rather than outside the House.
In view of all these considerations, I doubt very much that hon. members would expect the Chair to authorize the initiation of a debate on this matter which would eventually, perhaps, lead to the matter being sent to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I cannot see my way clear to ruling that there is a prima facie breach of parliamentary privilege, and I would not think the hon. member's motion should be put to the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not wishing to try your patience too much further, I have a regular and brief motion under Standing Order 43.
In view of President Pompidou's statement confirming France's determination to continue atmospheric nuclear tests in the South Pacific, and in view of the fact that Australia, New Zealand and a number of Latin American states have expressed united opposition to these tests, even to the point of threatening to withdraw diplomatic relations, I seek unanimous consent under Standing Order 43 to move the following resolution, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding):
Whereas continued testing of nuclear warheads by any nation anticipates a threat to human life on this planet, and
Whereas a yet unconfirmed report emanating from Australia that the Green peace crew has been incarcerated in a military hospital in Tahiti;
Therefore this House of Commons calls upon the government of France to cease all further tests and urges the Prime Minister to request immediately of the Ambassador of France that he confirm or deny whether or not the integrity of a Canadian vessel has been violated on the high seas.

subtopic: CANADIAN POLICY TOWARD GERMAN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC
CANADIAN POLICY TOWARD GERMAN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC
speechtext:
1.	Is the government considering granting MFN (most favoured nation) tariff treatment to the German Democratic Republic?
2.	Is the government considering the admission into Canada of trade commissioners from the German Democratic Republic?
3.	Is the government considering changing its policy of refusing to grant visas to journalists from the German Democratic Republic?
4.	Has the government been in negotiation with the German Democratic Republic regarding the above three matters?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Jerome (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN POLICY TOWARD GERMAN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC
speechtext:
I am informed by the departments of External Affairs, Industry, Trade and Commerce and Manpower and Immigration, as follows: 1. For the past two years, the Government has sought through unofficial means to put our trade with the GDR on a MFN (most favoured nation) basis.
2.	An unofficial arrangement providing mutual MFN treatment would facilitate consideration of any proposal for the establishment of an unofficial East German trade office in Canada.
3.	The Government has no policy of refusing visas to East German journalists. They come under the same regulations as any other visitor from the German Democratic Republic.
4.	Since Canada does not recognize the German Democratic Republic, there can be no contact at the governmental level. The Government of the German Democratic Republic is, however, aware of our position on these three questions.

The House resumed, from Tuesday, June 27, consideration of Bill C-5, to amend the Farm Credit Act, as report-
Farm Credit Act

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to say that as far as we are concerned the motion we are considering in the name of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) is very much in order and it is appropriate it should have been moved.
Indeed, when the bill was in committee I, personally, moved a very similar amendment. We adopted this approach because the bill gives the corporation power to carry out certain duties which have not been assigned to it by an act of parliament. It will exercise these powers by virtue of orders in council. We consider this would be allowing the government, and the corporation, too much latitude. Arguments were advanced ift committee in favour of the bill as it presently stands. We were told the corporation would have extensive powers anyway, that there would be $130 million at its disposal under votes 1 and 15, and that the corporation would have power to act without the benefit of these provisions in the bill in any case. I was a little disturbed that it should be so easy for the minister and the corporation to lay their hands on so much money and pursue policies which would appreciably affect the fate of many people involved in agriculture in the absence of what, to my mind, is proper control through legislation. So, regardless of the explanations given by those responsible at that time, I am still not ready to embody in an act this very loose enabling power which will give the government an opportunity to act without, to my mind, the necessary degree of responsibility to Parliament.
We were also told in the course of discussion that certain changes would, in any case, be necessary in connection with the farm adjustment program, now called the farm development program, and that it would be just as well if the board could carry on for a little while; after it had experimented, in effect, guidelines could then be laid down in legislation. But suppose that in the course of this experimentation one or two proposals do not work out very well and hardship or inequity arises. What recourse would individuals or communities have under the law? Could they go to the ordinary courts and say: "Certain things have been done which have cost me money, and I wish to recover the losses I have sustained"? They could hardly argue that certain things had been done which should not have been done under the terms of this or that Act of Parliament. As a legislator, I myself, for example, could not very well appear before the Standing Committee on Agriculture and say to the minister or to the representatives of the corporation that in a particular case they had taken action which did not conform with this or that section of the act. For these reasons, I do not believe the approach recommended to the House is a good one.
Anyone who observes the scene in agriculture today knows there are problems with which we must deal. At the same time, we must ensure that we act in such a way as not to aggravate those problems. One of the things which disturbs me is the lack of a clear indication of policy. The committee held several sittings, and a number of witnesses appeared. Finally, the minister came in and said: "Yes, we do have an updating of the statement made on March 8, 1972". I believe that was the date. But in any

June 28, 1972
Farm, Credit Act
case, whatever the date was, it was a long time before the information was available to us.
I must say I am bothered by the lack of balance in the policy as far as it has been explained to us. For example, there is provision for some subsidization of older people who choose to move out of farming; an annuity is to be paid to them, and so on. But I would have to learn a great deal more about the details of this proposal before I could either accept it or reject it. On the other hand, no assistance is provided for the younger person, or newcomers to agriculture who wish to establish themselves. In some European countries, interest rates are subsidized in such circumstances. The legislation before us ignores this aspect. It is considered quite all right to increase the total amount of a loan to $100,000, and that may be useful for those who want to borrow that sort of money. But for someone entering farming for the first time, the subsidization of the interest rate up to about half of the $100,000 is altogether justifiable. However, it is not even considered.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
No, we could not even get the amendment on the record, as the hon. member rightly says. It is not as though there were no subsidization policy in this country because there is. Under DREE, large subsidies are offered to private industry. I anticipate similar subsidies will be offered to industry to conform with antipollution laws. Students are subsidized through loans so they may attend college and university. The building of such institutions is also subsidized. Therefore, why should not persons entering agriculture be subsidized over the initial years, which are the tough years, while they are establishing themselves? If they turn out to be good farm operators and their income structure does not prove to be disastrous, they will turn their businesses into going concerns. The minister, who has lived in a farming community, knows that very well.
As I say, this need is ignored. We just assume that people will buy land, equipment and livestock, will become able and competent farmers and produce the food we need domestically and for export. I noticed that the other day the minister journeyed to Charlottetown in Prince Edward Island, and the main burden of the speech he made was that Canadians should produce food for export, that this assists the Canadian economy. I wonder whether the minister talked to the potato farmers of Prince Edward Island and received from them the assurance that they were in a sound financial position and would continue to produce potatoes? Did the minister also get the same feeling of confidence from farmers in the grain growing areas of Canada? I would ask also whether we have the same feeling of confidence about the general agreement on tariffs and trade, about our relations with the United States and our access to that important market. However, I do not want to digress.
Getting back to the bill, I am wondering whether those who drafted the bill clearly understand how it will be implemented and how well the two programs will dovetail together. On the one hand, we have a lending agency that has assisted farmers for a fair number of years on the
[Mr. Gleave.)
basis of their productivity and the management of their operation. We are now adding this social function. When you implement a policy that aims at the creation of farms of a certain size, you are performing a social function, not a commercial function. I suggest that, despite the usual pitfalls, a commercial lending operation is a fairly straightforward proposition. It is true you make bad guesses sometimes with regard to management or productivity, and you must take the good with the bad. However, if some able person is conducting the operation, over the long haul the operation will prove successful. As far as western Canada is concerned, despite the fact that western farmers experienced two or three low income years, I think it is fair to say they, too, will be successful. I suggest the Farm Credit Corporation has confidence that in the years ahead, as our cash flow increases and agriculture picks up again, our farmers will continue their operations satisfactorily. The minister and the Farm Credit Corporation realize that in the west there are good producing farms and there is good management.
However, the government has introduced a land development policy that is not only socially but politically motivated, and they will find that they are riding two horses which may very well be going at different speeds. As a result, the government are going to run into a fair bit of difficulty. I pointed out in committee that the bill provides that the appraised value of farmland shall be based as far as possible on its productivity. Yet the government is apt to use a different measure altogether, that of transferring farmer A to some other place and bringing in farmer B in his stead to operate his block of farmland. That is a different concept entirely.
The minister has run into some difficulty with the provinces, but I do not want to dwell unduly on that matter. I tried, as did other members of the committee, to get all the information I could on this matter as the bill was going through. Certainly, I do not want to criticize the minister for not getting agreement with the provinces. I assume he tried to, but I was not at the negotiations and do not know what happened. All I know is what I was told during the committee hearings. However, I suspect one reason there was a fair amount of difficulty in achieving agreement with the provinces was that what was proposed by the government in this area of land adjustment was ill-defined. The provinces, especially those which are largely dependent on agriculture, cannot afford to gamble on their future in that area. The income is very important to them and if farming operations are not in good shape, certainly in some cases the industrial base is not sufficient to make up for the mistakes made in the agricultural area. I would be much happier if we, as a committee and myself as a member, had more information on this matter. I know some of our people want additional amounts by way of loans. I know the needs of the farmers in my area fairly well, and the minister knows them across Canada.
I see you are getting uneasy, Mr. Speaker, so I assume my time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I should first like to thank the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and the hon. member for Prince Edward-
June 28, 1972

Hastings (Mr. Hees) for moving and seconding the motion yesterday on my behalf. I was unable to be here yesterday, as I was attending the opening ceremonies of the 28th annual meeting of the Indian Association of Alberta taking place at the Saddle Lake Reserve in my constituency. I thank the hon. member for Huron (Mr. McKinley) for explaining briefly the purpose of the motion I placed before the House for consideration. The purpose of the amendment is simply to restore parliamentary control over the possibility of any agricultural program being assigned to the Farm Credit Corporation for administration.
We have in Bill C-5 an amendment to Section 11 of the Farm Credit Act which broadens the powers and alters the functions of the Farm Credit Corporation, giving it the power to administer any kind of program that may be assigned to it by any other act of Parliament or by government order in council. It has been repeated many times in the committee by the minister and the Chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation that it is not necessary for this portion of the bill to be enacted to administer farm development programs. This arouses some suspicion. We wonder why we must have a clause in this bill which is all encompassing, broad and powerful.
There is no obligation under the provisions of this amendment to have an agricultural program approved or debated by Parliament. There is no obligation on the part of the government or the governor in council to discuss these programs or consult with the farmers of Canada or their organizations. There is not even an obligation for the government to produce a white paper or a position paper such as was produced under the provisions of the Small Farms Adjustment Program introduced on March 8. We wonder why we need such a broad and encompassing clause. We can only assume that the government may have some other mechanism which, in its wisdom, may alter the social and economic structure of agriculture.
During the consideration of this bill, and particularly of the adjustment program, we had a great deal of difficulty extracting information. An announcement was made of the government's intention in March, 1971, but we did not have a revised edition of the program presented to us until June 15 of this year, notwithstanding the fact that the bill was introduced on February 24, 1972. Throughout the course of the debate we tried to ascertain the direction in which the minister and the Department of Agriculture were proceeding. We have been and still are suspicious of the fact that this program will tend to reduce significantly the number of farmers in Canada, and we have evidence to back up that suspicion. Discussions and negotiations have been taking place with the provinces since the time the proposal was placed before the public. As I understand it, as of this date there has still been no agreement reached. Perhaps the minister will respond to that suggestion sometime later today.
We have been discussing this particular proposal in a vacuum. It was not until the provincial representatives appeared before the committee and took very strong exception to this bill, as did representatives of the National Farmers Union and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, although not as vigorously as other witnesses, that we had enough information to outline the
Farm Credit Act
main structure of the program. These representatives of the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan who appeared before the committee have serious reservations about the scope of the power granted in clause 1. The representative of the province of Manitoba stated explicitly in his brief, as recorded at page 6:
I have no recourse but to recommend to your Committee that the amendment to Bill C-5, extending the authority of the Farm Credit Corporation to administer such a program, be deleted from the Bill. Until such time as more satisfactory arrangements can be developed between the Federal Government and the provinces, I feel that the authority of the Farm Credit Corporation should not be extended to permit it to administer the proposed Small Farm Development Program.
The National Farmers Union, in an excellent brief, said basically the same thing. Let me quote from Committee Proceedings No. 22 of June 20 at page 22:4:
-the government, in our view, is being devious by circumventing public discussion and debate on the entire question of the Small Farm Adjustment Program while implementing an important part of the program in Bill C-5.
Certainly, so far as the NFU is concerned, there has been no communication from the Minister of Agriculture relative to further plans under the Small Farm Adjustment Program since his initial statement of March 8,1971.
It seems rather strange that a program which will very significantly affect, in some cases detrimentally, the farmers of Canada that little negotiation or discussion took place with a farm organization that speaks for the farmers of Canada.
Let me point out that the amendment to Section 11, as provided for in clause 1, does not only give power to the Farm Credit Corporation to administer the Small Farms Adjustment Program, but also any other duty or function assigned to it by the government by order in council. In other words, it can administer any agricultural program. In my opinion, and in the opinion of my colleagues, this power is much too broad for this or any other minister. The farmers of Canada have had some bitter experiences with some of the legislative measures introduced by this government, that is legislation drafted and introduced without any prior consultation with the farmers of Canada or their organizations. These pieces of legislation required many major amendments before they were acceptable, or indeed useful, to the farmers of Canada. They had to be changed by Parliament.
One could say that with the power which is to be delegated to the Farm Credit Corporation in this particular clause (1), Bill C-176 in its original form could have been administered by the Farm Credit Corporation had the government in its wisdom seen fit to assign to it a program of that nature rather than deal with it through legislation. We all know that after two years of parliamentary and public debate, the bill did pass but was altered significantly. It was altered to suit the wishes and needs of the producers who were affected. I suppose the same thing could be said about the stabilization bill which was certainly not in accord with the wishes of the vast majority of the farmers, according to the mail I have received and the public reaction generally.
With the power contained in clause (1), the government in its wisdom could have seen fit I suppose to assign the

June 28, 1972
Farm Credit Act
program under the stabilization bill to the Farm Credit Corporation for administration without parliamentary debate and without discussion with the producer organizations. So, I believe it behooves each and every one of us to think very seriously before we delegate this kind of authority to any kind of agency. In short, this clause would give the necessary power to reshape the social and economic structure of agriculture without reference to Parliament, without reference to the farmers of Canada, without reference to the provinces and without reference to the producer organizations. I recall that in the presentation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of the cabinet, the necessity was reiterated of producers being involved more closely and more meaningfully in the organization and development of programs as well as their evaluation.
Quite frankly, we believe this small farm adjustment program is tainted with the recommendations of the task force on agriculture which suggested that the number of farmers be reduced significantly in order to cure the ills of agriculture. We believe the major emphasis of a program such as the small farm adjustment program should be aimed at assisting those who are in the industry to improve their income and their standards, so that they may be able to remain in the field of agriculture and thus remain within the rural areas of Canada. This particular program does just the opposite. It is a program which encourages farmers to move out of agriculture. We recall that when the original proposal was presented by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) it was entitled an adjustment or redevelopment policy for agriculture, a proposal for farm adjustment and resource mobility. In the contents of the white paper, it was pointed out that one of the aims was to grease the wheels of adjustment.
I suppose because of the lack of acceptance of a title of that nature, the minister in his wisdom saw fit to rename the program the small farm development program. However, there is very little in that proposal to indicate it is a development program for small farms but rather is a development program for large farms. Perhaps it might be more appropriately called the small farm extinction program. We cannot accept a proposal which gives the government such carte blanche authority to proceed with any-and I want to emphasize the word "any"-detrimental or otherwise, agricultural programs which could affect the welfare of those engaged in the agriculture industry. I, therefore, propose that any such program which would affect the social and economic fabric of the agriculture industry should not be proceeded with by government order in council but rather by a bill which would be processed through the machinery of Parliament. Certainly, an ad hoc measure of this nature is neither desirable nor suitable.
I am sure all of us recall the ad hoc measure that was introduced to reduce wheat acreage entitled the Lift program. This was a stop-gap measure with an originally suggested expenditure of between $100 million and $140 million. Because this program was an hoc measure, it was introduced without any prior consultation or discussion with the farmers of Canada or indeed the farm organizations. Less than 50 per cent of the farmers of Western Canada were able to participate in the program and less

than 50 per cent of the funds allotted were expended. As a matter of fact, it discriminated against those farmers who had reduced their wheat acreage in the years prior to the introduction of this measure. Certainly, it was a very ill advised program. It was a bitter experience to many farmers of western Canada. Legislation which deals with the welfare, development or extinction of farmers in Canada should be clearly defined, clearly understood and introduced in Parliament as a piece of legislation rather than as a government order in council. Therefore, I urge all hon. members to accept this amendment which has been proposed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the committee on agriculture, we spent a considerable amount of time dealing with the different aspects and clauses of this particular bill. This amendment to section 11 of the Farm Credit Act, I suppose, in many ways has created the greatest controversy. I think the motion moved by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) is a commendable one and one which should be accepted by the House. Through a long process, we have seen different pieces of government legislation dealt with in terms of how they affected the farmer. We have seen debate centred around Bill C-197. After considerable debate, it ended up as Bill C-176. In that process there were no less than 6, 7 or 10 fundamental changes in the various provisions of the bill. We once sat all night at Christmas time- and I shall refrain from emphasizing this in case it should put you in a bad mood, Mr. Speaker-dealing with that legislation, and some rather fundamental changes were made in the government's proposal.
Now, in the second or third last day of the session we have the Minister of Agriculture bringing a bill before the House which, according to the amendment to section 11 of the Farm Credit Act, will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to administer any program the minister sees fit to allocate to it. My hon. friend moved a motion to delete this particular aspect of the proposed amendment to the Farm Credit Act. If we allow this amendment to pass as proposed by the minister, without accepting the deletion made by the hon. member for Vegreville, then we are giving a free hand to the Minister of Agriculture, regardless of who he is, to allocate whatever program he sees fit to the Farm Credit Corporation without giving the representatives of the people of Canada an opportunity to make a decision on that action. That, in the light of the activities of this government, can be a real threat to people in the rural areas.
In dealing with this amendment, I need only refer hon. members to the action taken by the government on the task force report on agriculture which stated that two out of every three farmers should be removed by 1990. There has been a drop in the number of farmers, and this has been a trend in agriculture for a long time. We all know that. The government is attempting to accelerate the removal of farmers from the land, in this case particularly those on small farms. This amendment allows the small farms consolidation plan to go into operation without any legislative authorization.
June 28, 1972

If the minister were still a member of the party which sits to my left, I wonder how he would have reacted to a Liberal government bringing in a bill that allowed plans and programs costing in the neighbourhood of $150 million over seven years to be put into effect without any authorization from the people's representatives. I wonder what he would have thought, and how it would have affected his constituency, if some minister of agriculture earlier in the history of this nation had carried out such a program.
What do we know of the small farm development consolidation plan? We know that it was introduced on March 8, 1971 as a resources mobility and adjustment program, not a development program. We have had a great deal of experience in listening to government ministers introducing programs with fancy names and no real intention behind them. Since that time we have not had a brief outline of exactly what the intent of that program is, other than what the minister called a corps program in committee. Only one provincial government has stated that it is in agreement with the plan as introduced by the Minister of Agriculture. Farm organizations, such as the National Farmers Union, have stated categorically, as the hon. member for Vegreville pointed out, that the method by which this program is being introduced is nothing short of devious, and that is the mildest word that can be used to describe the manner in which the minister has introduced the program. Under the program two farms would be made into one or three farms would be made into two. That is not a development of small farms, it is a development of bigger farms.
We find that the agricultural policies advocated by this government are continually overshadowed by the economics branch of the Department of Agriculture. I am sure that the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Whelan) does not appreciate the extent to which the economists control the Department of Agriculture and its policies. We are well aware of his opinions as expressed in the committee. First of all, on the basis of the task force report, the department made certain assumptions regarding the consolidation of farm holdings in terms of what they called efficiency. May I point out to the minister that farmers are more efficient and productive than Canadian industry. I do not understand how in the Lord's name he could ever introduce a consolidation program on grounds of efficiency. That is the purpose of the program. Part of the same concept of rationalization was the basis for the introduction of the incomes stabilization bill. If there had been a decision to administer that program through this amendment, members of this House would not have been allowed to have a public debate on that bill, the withdrawal of which would never have taken place and western producers would never have benefited from the savings.
I feel that this is a fundamental point, and I wish to repeat it regardless of the fact that the amendment deletes the provision relating to the small farm consolidation plan. Let us deal with the limited knowledge we have, with certain aspects of that particular program. First of all, the minister says that the program will be put into effect regardless of provincial agreement. This is very high sounding, and a beating upon one's chest before the federal election. It may sound good in some parts of the country. Let me point out to the minister that, as has been
Farm Credit Act
said in the committee, in terms of administration this program suggests the hiring of counselling personnel. That kind of counselling and advice is provided in almost every province with large rural areas, such as for example the Ag-Rep program in Saskatchewan.
I can tell the minister that if he thinks that the introduction of the small farms consolidation plan through this amendment will be a feather in his cap in the next federal election when the farmers know that he has added one more civil servant to the payroll to visit them, let me tell him that this plan will not go very far and neither will the minister. Not only are we setting up a program that cannot be examined by members of the House of Commons, but we are setting up an administrative bureaucracy which could affect each province in Canada where counselling and administrative services are already available, such as for example the Ag-Rep program in my province. Yet, the minister says that he is going ahead with it.
There has been some discussion about incentives being provided for farmers to leave their farms and to take up some other occupation. In view of the fact that there are 512,000 unemployed people in Canada, I am not sure what kind of employment they could expect. It has been mentioned that consideration must be given to those people going on welfare. I hope that the minister is well aware of the fact that in view of the lack of job opportunities in this country there seems very little opportunity for a man who has spent his life farming to suddenly train himself to be a technician in a chemical plant or to train himself for some other job which is usually non-existent anyway. Under this program there is no provision for the second, third or fourth son of a farmer who may have moved to the city and who wants to return to the land. This is where the social judgment comes in. Instead, there is a provision that the young farmer whose land, within the definition presented by this government, is uneconomic should be removed from the land. When I inquired about the possibilities in the Prairies for expansion I was told that he could find another quarter or half section of land but that might be 20 or 40 miles away and the cost was likely to put it out of his reach.
A program such as this would be impossible to administer because of the variation in the types of farming in the country. A small livestock or grain producer in my constituency of Assiniboia does not operate at all, in terms of land and costs, in the same way as a potato grower on Prince Edward Island or an apple grower in Nova Scotia. The average size of a farm in Saskatchewan, for instance, is much larger than the average size in Ontario, but in the small farm development consolidation plan there is no provision for such differences. Yet, Mr. Speaker, the minister says he is going ahead with it.
Mr. Speaker, I have given a number of reasons why I think the motion moved by the hon. member for Vegreville is a good one and I support it. I believe that he has a second amendment dealing with interest rates for young farmers. I am very interested in that and I hope it can be put to the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). Under Bill C-5 the Farm Credit Corporation may carry out virtually any program that the government of the day sees fit and this gives enormous power over an industry which already suffers from too much government interference. Apparently it is the stated intention of the government to use this clause of Bill C-5 to administer the small farm development program but, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that this program has been accepted or understood by the provinces. Indeed, from the minister's remarks I am not sure that he understands it, either. Any action in this area should be debated in Parliament so that members will have some idea of what is in store for the people. I think it is doubly important that legislation dealing with small farms should be thoroughly perused.
A study of what has happened in agriculture during the last four years shows how the government has intruded into the day-to-day business of farming. The Canadian Dairy Commission was in existence prior to 1968, but in that year it became much more active and since then it has substantially changed the pattern of the dairy industry in Canada. However, it has done this on a political basis rather than according to the demands of the market. As a result of high labour costs, many dairy farmers have switched to other products and the only way to get quotas for farm separated cream or milk is through the government or the Dairy Commission. The same situation now applies to eggs under Bill C-176 because quotas will be given to the provinces. Without a quota, a farmer cannot become involved in this industry. As far as chickens are concerned, the only way that a quota can be obtained in the broiler industry is from a commission. In Manitoba, a farmer can only raise 300 turkeys without a quota. If he raises more than that, he must obtain a quota from the provincial turkey board. Also in Manitoba a farmer without a quota for hogs is just out of luck. That leaves only cattle and sheep, the sheep industry is too small to get involved in quotas but the cattle industry is heading that way. In the western grain industry a lapsed quota has meant severe hardship for the small farmer who is prevented from taking advantage of some of the efficiencies available to his larger neighbour. Some of the Wheat Board's ideas with regard to grain deliveries are commendable, since the main thing is to get the grain to our customers. Some of their other ideas, however, have driven the small farmer to early retirement because of his economic situation.
As it stands, this clause of Bill C-5 would give the government power to do almost anything in order to carry out its program, and I believe this authority is far too wide, Mr. Speaker. We have heard only vague outlines of the small farm development program, Mr. Speaker. There is the assumption that the federal government will buy or in some manner rent or lease small farms, giving the owner an opportunity to take up another occupation or to retire with dignity. But, Mr. Speaker, no arrangement has been made to deal with the situation in the provinces. It should be realized that land use is under the jurisdiction of the provinces and will have to remain there under our concept of government. This is just another indication of

the federal government's centralistic approach to a problem which comes largely under provincial jurisdiction.
In their brief submission to the Standing Committee on Agriculture, the representatives of the National Farmers' Union said:
We believe members of this committee are fully cognizant of the effects of proposed amendments to raise upper limits on FCC loans to $100,000. Your endorsement of proposed amendments to Bill C-5 will signal your support of policies which advocate the continuing depopulation of rural areas and the sacrifice of the family farm to technology and economic determinism.
They then said that the bill does little for young farmers who need credit and that it fails to meet the needs of young farmers who wish to become established in farming. The government has not yet announced how small farmers under this legislation will have access to credit. Even if the amendment of the hon. member for Vegreville were to be incorporated in the bill, and even if the provisions of the bill applied to small farmers, we still would not know, and the government has not told us, how the small farms program is to be organized, how it is to be operated, and what its main thrust is to be.
This is an important measure and should not be dealt with in such general and vague terms. Until such time as the government comes forward with more definitive plans and proposals and defines more clearly what it means by the small farms program, I think this amendment ought to stand. We must be given a chance to debate any proposals the government has in mind for small farms.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the chance to speak in the closing portion of this debate. At the same time may I say that I support the amendment which would delete what we consider to be the contentious part of Bill C-5, the amendment brought forward by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski).
First, may I say that I agree in principle with that part of the Farm Credit Corporation bill which deals with increased amounts that are to be lent to farmers. The maximum amount to be lent is to be increased from $40,000 to $100,000. That sum is probably enough for one-owner farms. I should like to see a provision incorporated in the legislation which would raise the limit for farms owned by a corporation, which could be a family or a partnership. The maximum should be increased beyond the present limit for such farms. I think there is a legitimate reason for so doing, Mr. Speaker.
In the past year we have seen, and you will see to an accelerating extent in the future, and increasing emphasis on farm corporations on the Prairies and elsewhere in Canada. Farms have been incorporated, I suggest, because of our tax laws and because of the estate and gift taxes that many of us have had to live with in Canada. The government, in many cases, has forced the small businesses, and I certainly include many farms in that definition, to incorporate to escape succession duties that would need to be paid on the death of the person who established that particular farm or business enterprise. I should like to see the provision I have alluded to included in this bill or at least something along that line could have been included in the bill. In any event, I welcome the
June 28, 1972

increase in the ceiling, which is to be $100,000. At least under the Farm Credit Corporation legislation, farmers will be able to borrow that much and I think this bill will permit the Farm Credit Corporation to operate more effectively as a lending agency in the 1970's.
We must look realistically at farming, Mr. Speaker. When I say that, I do not want to leave the impression that I am in favour of larger farms and against small farms. As I say, in looking at agricultural problems, we must be realistic. Often we hear people say that the government must come up with positive measures for dealing with the small farm problem. Important though such measures may be, if we look at the picture positively and realistically and consider what shape farming will take in future, we will concede that, of necessity, farms should become larger. Any young farmer with managerial skills and ability to work hard will, as soon as he can, try to buy more land, because he will want a more viable economic unit. He will want to reduce his costs, and that is the most natural thing in the world. It is fine to talk about small farms and the preservation of the small farm in Canada. Until we can solve this problem, we shall, I think to a great extent, be just talking.
I think we should emphasize assisting farmers who want to remain on the land rather than making it easier for them to get off the land. I am talking of farmers with ability. One way to do this, I suggest-and I may be encroaching somewhat on the next motion that my hon. friend will propose-is by so structuring the Farm Credit Corporation that it will grant special loans to young farmers. These should be available in the first few years of farming when a farmer is seeking to become established. Possibly, repayments could be put off, and I am talking about interest and principal, for a few years until that young farmer gets on his feet. The mechanics of the loan could be worked out in such a way that the total amount of the loan would be paid back eventually. That would give the young farmer starting out a break. He would not need to repay borrowed money at once. This is important in view of the cash income situation of Prairie farmers. The government has been saying a great deal about this. It suggests that there is more cash in the hands of western Canadians now than there has been for some time. In view of rising costs and prices, Prairie farmers, despite their extra cash in hand, are considerably worse off than they were years ago. I feel we are justified in introducing some form of special credit facility for those young farmers who want to begin in the business. Such facilities should not be given to all segments of society; however, in view of rising costs, relatively low prices and the cost-price squeeze, such facilities I feel would be justified for young farmers.
Now, I come to the more contentious part of the bill. The amendment deals with a contentious matter. The small farms development program, as the government has called it, was introduced by the back door. Members of Parliament did not deal with that matter directly. All that we gleaned about the bill consisted of those small bits and pieces of information we were able to extract from the minister through answers to questions raised in the House of Commons of information obtained from press reports and of information contained in statements made outside the House. As a result, we became suspicious of the gov-
Farm Credit Act
ernment's intentions with regard to the small farms legislation. Only after extensive questioning in the committee that dealt with Bill C-5, and only after the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and the farmers unions had made every effort to discover the government's intentions, were we given a glimpse of what was in the package. There were not too many members who were in total agreement with what the government was proposing. One of the biggest problems we will see with the small farms development program will be the overlapping with provincial jurisdiction.
The province of Manitoba, in its submission to the committee, said that regardless of what happens to this legislation it will go ahead with its own legislation on small farms. We have heard the same story from oth^r provinces. The provinces are quite worried about the fact that there is no real flexibility in the program to meet the various needs of the different agricultural regions. There is a fear that a major emphasis in the program is placed on the readjustment of human resources out of agriculture. The provinces are also worried about the establishment of federal administrations in each province to administer the program, giving rise to overlapping with farm management and consulting services operated by the provinces themselves. The provinces are also worried about the fact that they had no say in the makeup of the small farms development program. They feel it was formulated by Ottawa and presented to them with the threat, "Either you take it or leave it We are not going to bend in any way so far as our proposals are concerned."
The fundamental issue that was outlined at the Edmonton meeting in July of 1971, attended by the other provinces, still remains. It concerns the federal government proceeding on a unilateral basis with a major program affecting Canadian agriculture, without permitting the provinces any say with respect to the kind of program that best suits their needs. In this respect we are seeing the hard core centralism or federalism that emanates from the present government It is not willing to negotiate with the provinces. I represent a riding in the province of Manitoba, and I know that province has additional concerns about details of the program which have not been outlined to any great extent in the House or even before the committee. I would like to mention one problem which will arise if the federal Department of Agriculture proceeds unilaterally with its program.
It was indicated earlier that a limit of $20,000 would apply to any property purchased under the land transfer program. The minister has stated that his department is still sticking with that figure, but there is a hint that this level could be raised through negotiations. But assuming that the level stays at $20,000,1 know that in the province of Manitoba much of the land covered by this program is land that the province itself does not want returned to agricultural use. This is just one example of the kind of problem the government will encounter if there is not further negotiation with the provinces.
Associated with this problem is the broader question of who will determine land policy within a province. All the provinces want to establish their own priorities in this matter, but it looks as though the federal government

June 28, 1972
Farm Credit Act
wants to have some say in determining provincial priorities. The provinces which made submissions noted that insufficient emphasis is placed on measures to assist farmers who wish to remain in agriculture. In fact federal officials have been emphasizing programs to assist farmers who wish to leave agriculture. This is one of the biggest concerns expressed by the majority of provinces with respect to the small farms development program. The fact is that the program is not flexible enough. The manner in which the federal government is trying to remove farmers from the land is not acceptable to western Canada or, indeed, to any part of Canada.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, once again I say that the amendments respecting dollar value, in so far as the FCC is concerned, are acceptable. They make the dollar value realistic for the 1970's. However, I think we should be able to deal fl/ith the small farms development program on a different basis. Toward the end of the committee hearings I believe the minister said a bill would be introduced after the program had been in operation. What use would a bill be at that time? This is completely unacceptable to most members on this side of the House. I urge all hon. members to support the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Vegreville, and I hope it will be carried when it is voted upon.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one of the most surprising pieces of legislation dealing with agriculture that I have seen since becoming a member of this House. The bill's provisions will modify the operations of the Farm Credit Corporation in several respects. In each case it is said that the changes being made will not necessarily affect the Farm Credit Corporation's operations as presently defined, with the exception of that provision governing an expansion of money, but the changes are being made so that the government can implement its new policy on small farm development.
During the last couple of years, Parliament has received several visitations from farm organizations that have been critical of the government's proposed program. All of the provinces have been unwilling to accept the small farms development program as outlined in a series of papers, I believe seven in total, of which only a couple are in the public domain. The Manitoba government, the Saskatchewan government, the National Farmers Union and other farm organizations have been highly critical of the proposed small farms development program, not knowing what its purposes are. One simple fact which is apparent to everyone is that size in itself is not necessarily advantageous. There is no one in this country who is not aware that size in itself is not necessarily an advantage. It may not even be advantageous to enterprises whose size approaches the upper limits.
I can recall one of my hon. friends asking, a few years ago: "What is wrong with a supermarket simply because it is big?" But we have seen supermarkets expanding to their present size without bringing any particular economic advantage as far as the consumer is concerned, though, no doubt, there is a great deal of return for those who finance these huge operations. So it may be with agriculture. I think of the largest farm units in my constituency.

In all cases they are operating on the basis of loans. Four or five of them have borrowed such large amounts that the local co-operative is in debt to the extent of $250,000. It cannot collect because the operators of those very large farms are so far in debt themselves that there is nothing to foreclose. Anyone who has advanced credit without attaching the land has no chance of getting the money returned.
There are advantages, of course, attached to the ability to procure extended credit. I am thinking of operations under the Dairy Commission through which amalgamations did take place; farms and quotas were purchased and this resulted in economic units being developed in my area. But this was not possible because the owners could borrow money or because their holdings had increased in size. It resulted from action taken by the government which produced a fair price for the product. It meant farmers were selling their product at profit and, within limits, the more they produced the more profit they could make. But if a farmer is producing wheat, for instance, and is selling at a loss, all he does if he doubles the size of his holding is to double the size of his loss. It is obviously not to a person's advantage to expand in those circumstances. He would be better off to maintain his holding and operate with the machinery he already possesses.
Representations made to us in connection with this bill suggest that the people themselves, in the area concerned, should have some say as to whether it would be advantageous socially or economically to amalgamate the smaller farms. If one farmer, whose production is uneconomic, buys a second farm which is in a similar position mainly because of the low prices received for the commodities produced, he will have acquired a larger unit, it is true, but it is very doubtful whether any real advantage has been secured.
I was interested in the charge made by representatives of the Farmers' Union that persons who are coaxed into borrowing more money are usually in difficulty already and that the borrowing of additional sums only means that some of this money, in a roundabout way, becomes income upon which the borrowers can live for a period. The government has on two occasions brought agricultural legislation before us to which the people directly concerned were opposed. One was the stabilization bill. Witnesses who appeared before the committee were of the opinion that this bill was detrimental to agriculture in general and to certain farmers specifically. The truth of their contention has now been borne out. Farmers are many millions of dollars better off in western Canada as a result of the stabilization bill not being passed.
Again, we are being warned by these same people that the legislation before us is not in the interests of the average farmer. Government spokesmen have offered very little by way of defence. What we are really doing is changing the terms upon which the Farm Credit Corporation operates. In line with this is the obvious intention of the Liberal party to reduce the number of farms in Canada. The Liberal party has pursued this intention for ten or more years, and it has never wavered in doing so. I am not sure that this is good policy. I know there are many farmers in eastern Canada who have remained in business only because the federal government intervened
June 28, 1972

to improve the price received for the commodity they produced. The only segment of the agriculture industry which is in reasonable shape today, the only segment I would recommend any young farmer to get into, is the milk production industry. This is the only agricultural enterprise which would warrant the borrowing of large sums of money. I say this because if a dairy farm is judiciously handled it will produce a better than average farm income.
When we talk about a farm development program we should obviously be talking about arrangements for young farmers entering the agriculture industry. This involves changes which the Farm Credit Corporation is not able to make on its own. There will need to be developments along the lines of a co-operative which will form conclusions as to the moral standing and agricultural ability of a young person and, if it is satisfied, lend him money, bearing in mind that he has time in which to repay it. Today money is lent to farmers 55 years of age. They Eire advanced sums of up to $100,000 though there is no possibility of their living long enough to pay off the debt.
I suggest that if we examine the amount of interest and premium payments made by farmers, it is doubtful that most of them would ever repay the premium amount before they die. Yet, we are making large loans to young farmers who are going into partnership with their fathers, which will mean that the junior member of the partnership will be mortgaged for the rest of his life, and perhaps for the lives of his grandchildren as well. I know of a case where, in my opinion, the mortgage on a farm is about twice the value of the goods and chattels on the farm and the land itself.
I do not think there is any other industry that offers an income so low that it is not possible to make a success of the operation. The average income of farmers across Canada is considerably less than $5,000, yet we are going to lend them money to enlarge their operations, to buy neighbouring farms, and in that way eliminate a very large proportion of our rural way of life. I, personally, know dozens of young people who have gone to cities to find work and have become immersed in an environment with which they are totally unfamiliar. In large part they have been given direction by the Department of Agriculture.
On the other hand, we make no attempt to give the farmers sufficient money to make a success of their operation and allow our young people to stay in rural communities where they can make a useful contribution. It is a fact that governments in Canada have always been plagued with the idea that they must create agricultural surpluses. No other industry offers its products in this way. However, I suggest there will be a day of reckoning if we continue to enlarge farm units but fail to take into account what those units can produce or to arrive at a reasonable price for those products.
Looking back over the past 20 years we find that the federal government has often maintained agriculture through payments out of the agricultural stabilization fund. We have disposed of our agricultural surpluses to countries around the world through the vehicle of a
Farm Credit Act
number of government agencies. We have made a national contribution in a number of ways by disposing of surplus production on our hands. And on a number of occasions, we have made efforts to arrive at a reasonable price. But it seems to me that the agricultural industry will never be a healthy one. Certainly doubling the size of farm units will not create a healthy agricultural climate. The only thing that will help agriculture is to give the farmers a reasonable price for the goods they produce.
I suggest that once this legislation has passed, the farmers should look at it very carefully before deciding whether to borrow further money from the Farm Credit Corporation. In my area, a number of people are anxiously considering another piece of farm legislation passed by the provincial government to establish a cow-calf operation. My advice to them is that if they have the buildings and sufficient land and machinery to go into a cow-calf operation today, they would probably be wise to borrow the capital required and increase their production considerably. But if they have to use the loan to amalgamate farm units before they can increase their production, or if they require buildings and other items of capital cost, then they are not going to make a success of the operation.
I suggest that we have already extended so much credit to the farmers that it would be foolish if they took advantage of further credit just because it was available. The farmers should consider very carefully whether borrowing money is the answer to their dilemma today. What is important is not the size of farm units or the farmer's capacity to produce, but the price he receives for what he produces, which is often below cost even in a well operated farm unit.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, might I rise on a point of order to ask whether the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) will indicate if he is going to accept this amendment? It might facilitate the passage of the legislation if he would say now that he will accept the amendment. The debate might then come to an end and we might have a vote. I am also wondering whether the minister plans to make a speech. I just raise those questions as a point of order.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to the debate, but as I said yesterday when the bill was reintroduced at the report stage, the amendment before us now is either identical to, or essentially the same as, one that was debated for several days in the standing committee, after which it was put to a vote and defeated.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not ask the minister for the opinion of the committee, I asked him for his opinion. At times his committee does not agree with him, and at other times he does not agree with the committee. I thought he could give us the position of the cabinet, which is not necessarily determined by the committee.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext: He does not have much say in the cabinet.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
The hon. member for Huron (Mr. McKinley) suggests that the minister has very little say in the cabinet, but I would not want to say that. I always hold out hope that any westerner in the cabinet has some power, though

June 28, 1972
Farm Credit Act
I might add that it appears to be a diminishing power to we westerners who sit close at hand and watch.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext: You do not complain about our increased wheat sales.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
Do not talk about rising wheat sales. It is the record demand for wheat in the world that has caused this increase. I am particularly pleased to see that we are not completely dead, and that our wheat sales for the year we have just finished studying increased 20 per cent over the previous year. This compares with the Australian increase of 32 per cent and the United States increase of 50 per cent. I would like to think our sales had increased even more. It is too bad we are not the leaders instead of running third, particularly when wheat plays such a dominant role in the income structure of so many farmers in western Canada. I wish our sales had increased to a greater extent and at a better price, rather than at a record low price. In fact, the realized net return on wheat to farmers in western Canada was the lowest in the last ten years according to the annual report of the Canadian Wheat Board which we finished studying late last night. If the hon. member who intervened would like to look at those figures, I can give him the page number of the report.
In Clause 1 of this bill we find the following:
The Corporation has all the powers necessary to carry out such duties or functions as may be assigned to it by the Governor in Council in relation to the administration of any agricultural program or as are assigned to it pursuant to any other Act of the Parliament of Canada.
This is a sort of ambiguous clause which leaves some fear in the minds of many members who are convinced that the governor in council some day may dream up another operation such as Lift, for example, and turn it over to the Crown corporation for administration. The Lift program was another matter that was never debated. Because of the demand throughout the world for wheat and feed grains this program has proven to be a gross error of tremendous magnitude, particularly in respect of farm income.
The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) announced in January that he had made a real breakthrough in that he was going to establish a realistic two-price system. Payments were to be made under a two-price system based on a dollar a bushel, and so on. What happened when Parliament reconvened? Slowly but surely, this idea seeped away. All of a sudden we heard there was not going to be any legislation, the government was just going to pay out the money in a one-shot program. Many farmers suspected the government was trying to buy their votes in the rumoured June election, or whenever it might be. Unfortunately for the Liberal party, the minister ordered the payments to be made but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did not call an election. Now, the Liberals are afraid that the farmers may spend the money before the election and not vote for the government, but these things happen.
The amendment spells out specifically that the corporation has all the powers necessary to carry out such duties

or functions in relation to the administration of any agricultural program assigned to it pursuant to act of Parliament. We feel there is some value in debate and in learning through the exchange of ideas. We have not given up on the concept of dialogue. We may have differences of opinion and violently disagree with what is going on in western Canada, in the Maritimes, in Newfoundland or in Quebec. We still agree that this shall be the meeting place of the representatives of the people and that dialogue will produce an exchange of ideas or a cross-pollinization. We feel this cross-pollinization will result in satisfactory answers to the problems confronting the people in various areas.
This particular bill seems to indicate that the Minister of Agriculture is afraid of dialogue and an exchange of ideas. He seems to be saying that we should not bother him too much because he has a television view and can only see in a straight line. We should not bother him with all the flack that comes through the process of debate. He wants to do what he wants, perhaps the creation of another Lift operation or acreage payments based on the two-price system so that votes will fall his way. He wants to build 2,000 boxcars but does not want debate, legislation or anything else which might let the people know who will be paying for those boxcars.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext: Are you against it?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
The hon. member can read the speech I made in the House of Commons on March 8 to find his answer to that question. He will see that I was not against it but suggested it.
In any event, it appears that the minister is afraid of debate. He is taking a negative approach. The minister, the Prime Minister and other Cabinet members go out to western Canada and ask the people what they want and why they are not satisfied. They say they are moving the grain, selling all kinds of it and want to know why they are not happy. They tell them they are building boxcars and they should be happy. We as the representatives of these farmers want to participate. Clause 1 of this bill will give the minister, through order in council, the right to bring in any kind of program he wants without consulting anybody except a few Liberal cronies back home, providing he has not become too high hat to speak even to them.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext: There are not too many of them anymore.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND POWERS AND CAPITAL OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member, there are not many of those old Liberal cronies left. This is how democracy is falling down, and this is how the parliamentary process is being eroded. We must not sit as legislators and allow such an all-inclusive clause to pass. Many members have read this all-inclusive clause and have come to the conclusion that this is how the small farm program gets into the picture. The minister has not really answered that question. He has said this would cover the small farm program, although it was not necessary because votes 1 and 15 of the estimates assure that this program will go ahead.
Much of the debate on Clause 1 has centred around small farm legislation. I was going to say this is propaganda, but it is even a little better than that. The minister put
June 28, 1972

forward this much talked about document on March 8, 1971, but since that time he has backed away from it. Some have suggested that the March 8 document indicated that the government would be purchasing land, along with other non-farmers. As a result of the minister's vacillation at committee meetings, we are in doubt as to whether the government will purchase land. I have asked the minister whether this is so and I hope he will answer before this debate is concluded.
Can non-farmers, who have no intent to farm, purchase land under this program for speculative or other purposes? Can they borrow money from the Farm Credit Corporation for the purchase of such land? There was a great deal of talk about the fact that the March 8 document indicated the small farm program would be available to senior farmers prepared to sell out when the farm land had a value of no less than $3,000 and no more than $20,000. The minister now says it is not tied to those values but is flexible. Someone asked whether the eligible value could go up to $35,000, and whether a portion of a farm rather than the whole farm could be sold. If a farmer were selling to his son, could he sell half the farm for $30,000 and lease the other half and receive the maximum grant? The minister has not answered these questions. He has suggested that the $20,000 limit will be raised, but he has not said how high. I asked him in committee if it would be raised to $35,000. He said it may, but that depended on the provinces.
As yet no province has agreed to go along with this program, and therefore the minister has categorically said that the government will not wait for the provinces but will proceed alone. Will a small farmer with a net real estate value on his farm of $35,000 qualify for the assistance to the elderly farmer who wants to sell out. That is about the fourth question I have asked to which I should like an answer. When I asked the minister if the small farms program was limited to the elderly farmer, he said that in his mind any farmer could receive the grant but that he preferred to think it would be given to a farmer who was elderly and wished to enjoy a higher quality of life somewhere else. Such a farmer would be given assistance. The minister said there would be a direct grant of $1,500 to such a farmer who would be selling out, plus 10 per cent of the sale value of the farm. If the maximum value were $20,000 this would mean a grant of $3,500. This is the bonus that would be received by a farmer who retires from the land who seeks, in the minister's words, a higher qualify of life in another occupation.
The other question which has not been answered is in respect of a young person or another farmer buying land and receiving special consideration. Would he be able to buy it under conditions which would allow him a lower down payment than if the program were not in effect? I do not think that question has been answered. We are led to believe the House plans to adjourn at the end of this week. If I were in the minister's place, I would be inclined to try to co-operate in answering these questions. This may be the last piece of legislation the minister will have the privilege of bringing into this House of Commons, the good Lord willing. I think if I were in his place I would be very co-operative with the House and try to answer these
Farm Credit Act
questions. In this way the minister would have an opportunity to have his name recorded in posterity as one who put forward one more piece of legislation. These are the four or five questions I have in respect of this legislation.
I have before me the Federal Farm Credit and Related Statistics booklet. In this booklet there is a table which sets out the class of FCA borrowings by province. Without going into the matter of the provinces, the number of loans made on farms with a net value of land worth $20,000 represented 4.7 per cent of the number of borrowers. So, up until this date we are dealing with a very small section of borrowers. Does the minister hope to enlarge this section? Is the program geared to encourage the small farmers to borrow more money in order to buy land or, as suggested by the National Farmers Union in the committee, is this program designed to take agricultural land out of production? Is it designed to lend the money to nonfarmers who will use it perhaps for the purpose of subdividing the land into what are called acreages on the edge of major cities or for the purpose of light industry. Is this the concept under which a farmer who has been producing, let us say, a fair return or a fair amount of money per acre will find that his acreage is to be used to pasture one saddle horse for the young children in a family rather than being used to produce products to be sold abroad. This is a question in the minds of many people. We on this side of the House go along with the over-all concept of lending more money to farmers. One has only to look at the difficult plight in which many farmers find themselves.
In the same booklet at page 63 there is an interesting table in respect of land tenure by province. Let us take, for example, the province of Alberta. There is much concern today about Americans buying up Canadian land and so on. In the province of Alberta in 1961, 51.5 per cent of the agricultural land was farmed by the owner of the land. In 1966, this figure increased to 62 per cent. I think this is a good direction in which to be going. In the province of Saskatchewan, however, the reverse is true. In 1961, 64.9 per cent of the land was farmed by the owner. In 1966, this figure had reduced to 55.4 per cent, nearly 10 per centage points in a five-year period. In other words, more farmers were leasing or renting land in that province rather than owning it. I might as well give the figures for the province of Manitoba. In 1961, 80 per cent of the land was farmed by the owner. In 1966, the figure had reduced to 65.8 per cent. This is a trend of which I do not believe anyone should be particularly proud. It is interesting to note in that same table that for the remainder of Canada the percentage is much higher, in the 88 per cent and 89 per cent bracket, and remains relatively constant in that five-year period in comparison to the three prairie provinces.
Because of its application to very low net worth farms, this small farms program will not be very beneficial to the areas which perhaps need it the most. If it were necessary to pass judgment on the small farms program, it might be considerably different from the judgment on Bill C-5 because Bill C-5 does two things. It allows the Farm Credit Corporation to lend more money to the individual and to a younger individual. It reduces the age of the borrower from 21 to 18. I think these two things are beneficial. Clause (1), in its all-encompassing provision,

June 28, 1972
Farm Credit Act
takes in the small farms program and it is regrettable that the minister has not given a more complete and clear explanation of what he really envisages. Is it to reduce the number of farms? Is it really a farm adjustment program or a farm development program? Is it to place more farmers on the land who will be better able to provide for themselves or is it to have less farms on the land? These questions should be answered before this minister and this House ask us to pass this legislation during the dying minutes of this session.
